953.title: Three times
953.hook: Peter denied Jesus three times; after the resurrection he is asked three times, lovest thou me? (John 21:15–17)
953.howItsDone: In Christian teaching, John 21 is read as the restoring of Peter after his denial, and some preachers draw attention to the two fires of coals that frame the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zacchaeus came down from the tree and gave back more than he took. Your line was fourfold. What did you repay? Today, a new week, and a friend who failed at the worst moment. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

I am not. Three short words, said in a courtyard at night, and it's cold. Servants and officers have made a fire of coals, and they're standing around it warming their hands. Peter is standing with them. Inside, Jesus has been arrested and is being questioned. A girl at the door looks at Peter and asks if he's one of this man's disciples. He says no. Then someone else asks. Then someone else. Three times, he says no. And then the rooster crows. Today: three times.
screen: `A FIRE OF COALS.` → `I AM NOT.` → `THREE TIMES, THEN THE ROOSTER.`

segments.voice: First, the failure. Peter isn't a stranger to Jesus. He's the one who said he would lay down his life for him. And when it counted, he warmed his hands by someone else's fire and said he didn't know him. Luke adds a detail that's hard to read: "the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter." And then: "Peter went out, and wept bitterly." No speech. Just a look, and a grown man crying outside. Second, the second fire. Turn to the end of John's Gospel. After the resurrection, some of the disciples have gone back to fishing. They come in at dawn and find Jesus on the shore, and John says: "they saw a fire of coals there." The same picture as the courtyard. A fire of coals. Breakfast is cooking on it. Third, the three questions. After they eat, Jesus turns to Peter: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?" Peter says: "Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee." Jesus says, "Feed my lambs." Then he asks again. And a third time. John says Peter was grieved because he was asked the third time. Three denials, three questions. Every no in the courtyard gets a yes by the fire. Fourth, the job. Each time Peter answers, he gets work: feed my lambs, feed my sheep. Not probation. Not a lecture about the courtyard. Jesus doesn't mention the denial at all. He gives the man who failed the care of the others. Some Christians call this scene the restoring of Peter, and its shape is simple: the second chance comes with a real task, handed over by the fire.
screen: `DENIAL BY THE FIRE.` · `A SECOND FIRE OF COALS.` · `THREE TIMES: LOVEST THOU ME?` · `FEED MY SHEEP: A REAL TASK.` · then, large: `THOU KNOWEST THAT I LOVE THEE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go. Think of someone who let you down and has been trying, in their own clumsy way, to come back. A friend who flaked. A sibling who said the wrong thing. A child, a parent, a colleague. Picture them by a small fire, asking if things can be all right. Now notice what you've been doing: keeping them at the door, or letting them in? Imagine giving them one real chance to make it right, a small task, a bit of trust. If the person who failed is you, picture being asked the question and answering yes. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Three times. Peter's three denials in the courtyard, and his three answers by a fire on the shore: thou knowest that I love thee. Today's word.
Your line: a second chance. Today, let someone who let you down make it right: give them one small, real way to do it, and let them. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

pairs: feed my lambs, feed my sheep

myth: Jesus brings up the denial and makes Peter apologize
he never mentions it; he asks lovest thou me, and gives Peter work.
John uses the same picture, a fire of coals, in both scenes
a fire of coals in the courtyard, and a fire of coals on the shore.
Peter was grieved when he was asked the third time
John says so directly: he was grieved because he said unto him the third time.

fork.setup: you're Peter, eating breakfast on the shore with the one you denied three times. what does Jesus say to you?
options: he reminds you of the courtyard.
he asks, lovest thou me?
he tells you to go home.
fork.reveal: he asks three times, "lovest thou me?" and each yes is answered with a job: feed my lambs, feed my sheep.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter got caught lying and felt bad.
what it means: three denials undone by three questions, and a second chance that comes with real work.

what a scholar hears: some readers notice John repeats one detail, a fire of coals in the courtyard and a fire of coals on the shore, so the restoring happens beside the same kind of fire as the failing.

954.title: The guard's hand
954.hook: Corrie ten Boom, who lost her sister in Ravensbrück, later took the hand of a former guard (The Hiding Place, 1971)
954.howItsDone: Christians retell Corrie ten Boom's story, from her memoir The Hiding Place, when speaking about forgiving those who did terrible harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter by two fires, and three questions that answered three denials. Your line was a second chance. Who did you let make it right? Today, the Christian voices step out of scripture and into living memory. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

A church in Munich, after the war. A Dutch woman named Corrie ten Boom has just finished speaking about forgiveness. People are filing out. One man comes forward instead, smiling, with his hand held out, grateful for her message. And she knows his face. In her memoir, The Hiding Place, she tells what came back in that instant: the camp called Ravensbrück, the uniform, the shame of the processing room, and her sister Betsie, who died there. He doesn't seem to remember her. She remembers him. His hand is still out. Today: the guard's hand.
screen: `A CHURCH IN MUNICH.` → `A HAND HELD OUT.` → `SHE KNOWS HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: First, who she was. In The Hiding Place, Corrie tells how her family, Christian watchmakers in the Dutch city of Haarlem, hid Jewish people in their house during the Nazi occupation. They were betrayed and arrested. She and Betsie were sent to Ravensbrück. Betsie, in Corrie's telling, kept talking about forgiveness even in the camp. She did not come home. Second, the moment. In the church, the former guard tells her how grateful he is for her message, that his sins are washed away. Corrie, who has just preached that very message, finds she can't lift her hand. She describes anger and a wish for revenge rising in her, and knowing they were wrong, and being unable to make them go away. That honesty is the heart of the story. The one who taught forgiveness found she couldn't do it on her own. Third, the prayer. In her account, she prays silently, telling Jesus she can't forgive him, and asks for the forgiveness she doesn't have. Then she takes his hand. She describes something like a current running between them, and a love she says was not her own. In her telling, that is the point: forgiveness came as something given to her, not something she produced. Fourth, what it doesn't claim. She doesn't say it was easy, or that the camp didn't matter, or that Betsie's death was somehow fine. She tells it as a struggle she lost before help came. Jesus's own words in Matthew stand behind her: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you." Her story doesn't make that command smaller. It shows how heavy it is, and that one person, at least once, carried it across a church aisle.
screen: `A FAMILY THAT HID NEIGHBORS.` · `SHE COULDN'T LIFT HER HAND.` · `A PRAYER: I CANNOT, GIVE ME YOURS.` · `HARD, NOT SMALL.` · then, large: `LOVE YOUR ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: Take a slower breath than usual, and then another. This one asks for care. Let a very hard forgiveness come to mind, only if you're ready. It might be your own, or someone else's you've watched from close by. You don't have to forgive anything today. Just be honest the way Corrie was: notice what rises when you think of it. Anger, grief, numbness, all of it. Let it be there. Then ask one small question: what would it take, even for a moment, to make this possible? If you pray, you can do what she did and ask for help with what you can't do alone. The bell holds the time.
Ravensbrück. The camp where Corrie ten Boom's sister died, and where the guard whose hand she later took had served. Today's word.
Your line: hard, and possible. Today, when a forgiveness feels impossible, don't force it. Just say the honest thing to yourself: this is hard, and maybe not impossible. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

a former guard, hand held out
I cannot; give me your forgiveness

she says she couldn't lift her hand, and had to ask for help.
the ten Boom family hid Jewish people in their house
that's why they were arrested and sent to the camps, in Corrie's telling.
in her account, the forgiveness felt like her own achievement

fork.setup: you're Corrie. a former guard from the camp where your sister died holds out his hand to shake yours. what does she do first?
options: takes his hand at once.
stands frozen, unable to lift her hand.
walks away without a word.
fork.reveal: she can't lift her hand. only after a silent prayer for help does she take it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saintly woman who forgave easily.
what it means: someone who taught forgiveness found she couldn't do it alone, and asked for help.
what a scholar hears: Corrie's own account doesn't hide the anger; the story's force is the gap between the message she preached and the hand she couldn't lift.

sources.ref: The Hiding Place (Corrie ten Boom with John and Elizabeth Sherrill), closing chapter

955.title: Nickel Mines
955.hook: in 2006 an Amish community in Pennsylvania publicly forgave the man who shot their children, and comforted his family
955.howItsDone: Amish Christians pray the Lord's Prayer and take its line about forgiving others as something to practice; in the book Amish Grace, Amish people interviewed describe forgiveness as giving up revenge, not forgetting the loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ravensbrück, and a hand held out in a Munich church. Your line was hard, and possible. Which hard thing did you let yourself name? Today, the last of the Christian voices this block, and a whole community facing the hardest forgiveness. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

Nickel Mines is a small place in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, with farms, buggies and a one-room Amish schoolhouse. One autumn morning, a man from the area, not Amish, walked into that school with guns and shot girls in their classroom, and then himself. This lesson won't linger on the details. What it remembers is what came next. Within hours, Amish neighbors went to the gunman's family. Not to accuse. To comfort them. Today: Nickel Mines.
screen: `A ONE-ROOM SCHOOLHOUSE.` → `A MORNING OF GRIEF.` → `NEIGHBORS GO TO HIS FAMILY.`

segments.voice: This account follows the book Amish Grace, written by scholars who studied the community's response. First, the visits. The book describes Amish neighbors going to the gunman's widow and his parents in the first days, to say they held no grudge, and to sit with them. Amish neighbors, it says, were among the mourners at his burial, standing with the family of the man who had done this. Second, the gifts. Gifts of money came in for the Amish families. The book tells how the community shared some of it with the gunman's widow and children, who had lost someone too and had done nothing wrong. Those are the other family. Third, where it came from. The authors trace the response to the Lord's Prayer, which the book describes as prayed daily in Amish homes, and to Jesus's words right after it in Matthew: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." The same line these Christian voices began with. For the people of Nickel Mines, in the book's telling, that verse wasn't a nice idea. It was something you do, even here. Fourth, what forgiveness didn't mean. The book is careful about this. The families grieved, deeply and for a long time. Forgiving didn't erase the loss, or call what happened anything but evil. It meant giving up the right to revenge, and refusing to let bitterness take over. Some outsiders praised it; some questioned whether it came too fast. The authors take both reactions seriously. What's left is a plain picture: grieving parents sitting with a widow, remembering that the man who did this also left behind a family.
screen: `NEIGHBORS AT HIS FAMILY'S DOOR.` · `GIFTS SHARED WITH HIS WIDOW.` · `IF YE FORGIVE MEN THEIR TRESPASSES.` · `GRIEF STAYS. REVENGE GOES.` · then, large: `THE OTHER FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Before anything else, take a few slow breaths. This practice is gentle on purpose. Think of someone who has caused harm, close to you or far off in the news. Don't focus on them. Turn instead to the people around them: a parent, a partner, a child. People who didn't choose what happened, and who carry it anyway. Picture one of them at a kitchen table, alone with it. Let a small wish rise for that person: some peace, some company, someone at the door. If you pray, you can hold that family in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Nickel Mines. The Amish community in Pennsylvania that, after a shooting at its school, went to comfort the gunman's family. Today's word.
Your line: the other family. Today, when you hear of someone who did harm, give one thought to the people who love them and are carrying it too. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

956.title: Despair not
956.hook: despair not of God's mercy, for God forgives all sins (Quran 39:53)
956.carry: even if your sins reached the clouds
956.howItsDone: Muslims seek God's forgiveness, called istighfar, in prayer and in their own words, and call on God by names such as al-Ghafur, the Forgiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nickel Mines, and neighbors at a grieving door. Your line was the other family. Who did you give a thought to? Today, the Christian voices give way to Muslim voices, starting with a verse of the Qur'an. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

Two in the morning, and somebody is awake, replaying something they did years ago. A word said in anger. A friend let down. A thing nobody else knows about. It has been forgiven by others, maybe, or forgotten by them. But not by the one lying awake. There's a voice in that kind of night that says: too late, too much, this one stays. The Qur'an has a verse spoken straight into that voice. It doesn't start with a rule. It starts by naming the people it's talking to. Today: al-Ghafur.
screen: `AWAKE AT TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `TOO LATE, TOO MUCH.` → `A VERSE SPOKEN INTO THAT VOICE.`

segments.voice: First, who it's for. The verse opens with a command to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to speak in God's name. In Pickthall's translation: "Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt!" Prodigal, here, means people who have gone too far, wasting themselves, hurting their own souls. Notice the word My. Not those people: My slaves, belonging to God. The ones who went too far are still addressed as His. Second, the command. "Despair not of the mercy of Allah." Notice what's being forbidden. Not the wrong, at least not in this line. Despair. The verse treats hopelessness about mercy as its own kind of mistake, as if to say the door is not the problem; believing it's locked is. Third, the reach. The verse continues: "Who forgiveth all sins." All. The next verse calls people to turn to their Lord and surrender to Him before a reckoning comes, and the promise is read together with that turning back. Read that way, the mercy isn't a reason to stop caring. It's a reason not to give up. Fourth, the name. The verse ends: "Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." The Forgiving, in Arabic, is al-Ghafur, one of the names Muslims use for God. There's a saying of the Prophet, recorded by at-Tirmidhi, that puts it vividly: in it God says that even if a person's sins reached the clouds of the sky, and they asked forgiveness, God would forgive them. For Muslims who pray with this verse, it answers the late-night voice that says too late with two words: despair not.
screen: `O MY SLAVES: STILL CALLED MINE.` · `DESPAIR IS WHAT'S FORBIDDEN.` · `ALL SINS, AND A TURNING BACK.` · `THE FORGIVING, THE MERCIFUL.` · then, large: `DESPAIR NOT OF THE MERCY OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop, and breathe out a little longer than you breathe in. Let one old guilt you still carry come up. Something already done and over, that you've said sorry for or can't fix now. Hold it the way the verse holds the people it speaks to: as someone who went too far, and is still called by name. Notice the voice that says it's too late. Don't argue with it. Just set the verse's two words beside it: despair not. Breathe out, and let the weight loosen a little, even if it doesn't leave. If you pray, you can ask forgiveness in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Al-Ghafur. The Forgiving, a name for God in Islam, from the verse that tells those who went too far: despair not. Today's word.
Your line: even if your sins reached the clouds. Today, when an old guilt comes back, answer it with that line, and let one thing go that you've already made right. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

options: not to pray until they've made amends.

fork.reveal: "despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." the thing forbidden here is hopelessness.

original.note: Arabic: the Forgiving, as Qur'an 39:53 names God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse saying anything goes.
what it means: a word to those who went too far: you are still called Mine, and despair is the mistake.
what a scholar hears: the verse opens with Say, a command to the Prophet, and is read together with the next verse's call to turn back.

957.title: The Prophet at Ta'if
957.hook: stoned out of the town of Ta'if, the Prophet refuses to curse its people and prays for their descendants
957.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Ta'if, from the hadith and the early biographies, as an example of the Prophet's mercy; teachers use it when speaking about answering rejection without revenge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, and a verse telling people who have wronged themselves not to lose hope of God's mercy. Your line was even if your sins reached the clouds. Where did you set down an old guilt? Today, a road out of a town that threw a man out. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.
screen: `EVEN IF YOUR SINS REACHED THE CLOUDS.`

segments.voice: A road leading away from a hill town, and a man walking it, hurt and slow. Behind him, a crowd is still shouting. He had come to the town of Ta'if to speak to its leaders. The early biographies say they refused him, and then set people along the road to jeer at him as he left; some tellings add stones. He reaches the shade of an orchard and sits down. This is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. What happens further down that road, as he himself later told it, is what this day is about. Today: the Prophet at Ta'if.
screen: `A ROAD OUT OF A HILL TOWN.` → `STONES FROM THE ROADSIDE.` → `SHADE IN AN ORCHARD.`

segments.voice: First, the hardest day. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, his wife Aisha asks whether he ever faced a day harder than the battle of Uhud. He says his people had hurt him badly, and the worst was the day he went to Ibn Abd Yalil, a chief of Ta'if, and was turned away, and walking on so troubled that he only came to himself further down the road. Second, the offer. In the same report, he looks up and sees a cloud, and in it the angel Gabriel, who tells him God has heard how the people answered him, and has sent the angel of the mountains. That angel greets him and offers, if he wishes, to bring the mountains together on the town. A complete answer to everything that just happened. Third, the refusal. He says no. In paraphrase, he says he hopes God will bring out from their descendants people who worship God alone. Not a curse. A hope, aimed at children not yet born. The people who drove him out are left standing, and their grandchildren are given a future in his words. Fourth, where the story comes from. The jeering crowd on the road comes from the sira, the early biographies of the Prophet. The angel and the answer come from the hadith. Muslim teachers tell it as a picture of mercy at the very moment the power to answer was in his hands. He had been humiliated. He was offered the means to settle it. He chose the longer view.
screen: `THE HARDEST DAY.` · `THE ANGEL OF THE MOUNTAINS.` · `NO: THEIR CHILDREN INSTEAD.` · `WHERE THE STORY COMES FROM.` · then, large: `NOT A CURSE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one person, or one group, who turned you away. A job that said no. A friend who closed the door. A family that didn't make room. Don't replay the scene. Just see their faces for a moment. Then, in place of the old sentence you usually say about them, try a wish that reaches past the hurt: that things go well for them, or for the people who come after them. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own tradition's words. If you don't, just hold the wish. The bell holds the time.
Ta'if. The town that drove the Prophet out, offered the mountains in answer, and given a hope for its children instead. Today's word.
Your line: not a curse. Today, when the name of someone who once shut you out comes up, let the next thing you say about them be not a curse. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

fork.reveal: he said no, and hoped God would bring from their descendants people who worship God alone. not a curse: a hope for children not yet born.

original.note: Arabic: Ta'if, the hill town that turned the Prophet away.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophet who never got hurt or turned away.
what it means: he named it among his hardest days, was offered revenge by an angel, and said no.

sources.work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq, in Ibn Hisham's recension)

958.title: No blame today
958.hook: entering Mecca, the Prophet echoes Joseph: no blame on you today (Quran 12:92)
958.howItsDone: Muslims read Joseph's words in surah 12 and tell the sira's account of the Prophet repeating them at Mecca; the phrase is quoted when people are urged to forgive old enemies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Prophet at Ta'if: offered the mountains, he hoped for the town's children instead. Your line was not a curse. Whose name did you speak of more gently? Today, the same man walks back into the city that drove him out. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

What do you say to the people who pushed you out of your home, on the day you walk back in and could do anything you like to them? The early biographies say the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, faced exactly that. Years after leaving Mecca, he returned with a large following, and the city opened to him. The men who had mocked him, fought him and driven his followers away were gathered, waiting to hear what would happen to them. Tradition says he didn't make up a new answer. He borrowed one from an older story. Today: no blame today.
screen: `THE CITY THAT DROVE HIM OUT.` → `THE OLD ENEMIES, WAITING.` → `AN ANSWER BORROWED.`

segments.voice: First, the older story. In the Qur'an's surah of Joseph, Joseph's brothers throw him into a well, and he is sold away. Much later he is a powerful man in Egypt, and the brothers come before him needing grain, not knowing who he is. When at last he tells them, they admit they were in the wrong. Second, his answer. The Qur'an gives his words at chapter twelve, verse ninety-two. In paraphrase: there is no blame on you this day; may God forgive you, and he is the most merciful of those who show mercy. Notice what he doesn't do. No speech about the well. No list of what it cost him. The case is closed in a sentence, and the rest is handed to God. Third, the echo. In the sira, the story goes that when Mecca opened to him, the Prophet asked the Quraysh, his own tribe, what they expected from him. In the telling, they answered that they expected good from a generous brother. And he answered with Joseph's words. Tradition adds that he told them to go, that they were free. Fourth, what the line does. A grudge is a case kept open, filed and ready to be pulled out. No blame today closes it, on a day you can name. It doesn't say nothing happened; Joseph's brothers knew exactly what happened, and said so. It says the account won't be pressed. And it comes from someone who had every means to press it.
screen: `JOSEPH AND HIS BROTHERS.` · `NO BLAME ON YOU THIS DAY.` · `THE PROPHET BORROWS THE LINE.` · `A CASE CLOSED ON A NAMED DAY.` · then, large: `NO BLAME TODAY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow down. Bring up one grudge you've kept open. Not the biggest one. One you know the shape of. Picture it as a file on a desk, the evidence all in order. Now, without arguing the case again, close the cover. Say to yourself, quietly, the name of today. Not that it didn't happen. Just that from today, the account isn't pressed. If you pray, you can hand the rest to God in your own tradition's words. If you don't, set the file down and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Quraysh. The Prophet's own tribe, asked what they expected from him when Mecca opened to him, and answered with Joseph's words. Today's word.
Your line: the account won't be pressed. Pick one grudge and close it, by name and by date. If it comes knocking tomorrow, the date still stands. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

959.title: Abu Bakr's cousin
959.hook: Abu Bakr stopped supporting a relative who slandered his daughter, and a verse asks him to forgive (Quran 24:22)
959.carry: wouldn't you love to be forgiven
959.howItsDone: Muslims read Qur'an 24:22 with the account of Abu Bakr and Mistah, and it is cited to encourage people not to cut off support to relatives who have wronged them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Quraysh asked what they expected, and no blame today: Joseph's words to his brothers, carried into Mecca. Which grudge did you close? Today, a quieter forgiveness, inside one family, over money and a lie. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

A household allowance, cut off. That's where this story starts. Abu Bakr, the Prophet's friend and father-in-law, had long been providing for a poor relative named Mistah. Then a rumor went round Medina accusing Abu Bakr's daughter Aisha, the Prophet's wife, of something she hadn't done. Mistah was one of the people who spread it. When Aisha was cleared, Abu Bakr swore he would never give Mistah anything again. It sounds fair. A verse of the Qur'an asked him a question instead. Today: Abu Bakr's cousin.
screen: `AN ALLOWANCE CUT OFF.` → `A LIE ABOUT AISHA.` → `AN OATH, AND A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the hurt. This isn't a stranger's insult. Mistah ate at Abu Bakr's expense and used his tongue against Abu Bakr's own child. Aisha's long account of these days, in Sahih al-Bukhari, describes her weeping through the nights before she was cleared. Abu Bakr's oath is easy to understand. Second, the verse. Qur'an chapter twenty-four, verse twenty-two. In paraphrase: let those among you who have grace and means not swear off giving to their relatives, the poor, and those who left their homes for God's cause. Let them pardon, and overlook. Wouldn't you love God to forgive you? And God is forgiving and merciful. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't call Mistah innocent. It doesn't ask Abu Bakr to pretend. It asks him not to let the wrong cut off the kindness. Third, the question. The verse could have simply ordered it. Instead it turns Abu Bakr around to face his own need: wouldn't you love to be forgiven? Fourth, his answer. In Aisha's account, Abu Bakr says yes, by God, he would love God to forgive him, and he goes back to providing for Mistah as before. Look back at this week: a disciple asked three times, a guard's hand taken, a village comforting another family, a verse against despair, a road out of Ta'if, no blame today. This one looks the smallest. An allowance restored. It may also be the one closest to ordinary family life.
screen: `A LIE ABOUT HIS DAUGHTER.` · `PARDON, AND OVERLOOK.` · `WOULDN'T YOU LOVE TO BE FORGIVEN?` · `THE ALLOWANCE RESTORED.` · then, large: `WOULDN'T YOU LOVE TO BE FORGIVEN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Think of one kindness you've quietly withdrawn from someone after they let you down. A ride you stopped offering. A text you stopped sending. An invitation that no longer goes out. You don't have to decide they were right. Just look at the kindness itself, sitting unused. Then ask the verse's question, gently, of yourself. And picture handing that one kindness back, just once. If you pray, you can bring the question to God in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Mistah. The poor relative who helped spread a lie about Aisha, and whose support was restored after a verse asked a question. Today's word.
Your line: wouldn't you love to be forgiven. Today, restore one small kindness you quietly stopped: the text, the ride, the invitation. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

match.prompt: Abu Bakr's cousin — tap the pairs.
pairs: a poor relative who spread the rumor

myth: the verse declares that Mistah did nothing wrong
it doesn't. it asks Abu Bakr not to let the wrong cut off his giving.
the verse asks a question instead of only giving an order
wouldn't you love God to forgive you?

fork.setup: you're Abu Bakr. a relative you've long provided for helped spread a lie about your daughter. she's been cleared. what do you do?
options: never give him anything again.
restore his support.
demand a public apology first.
fork.reveal: he had sworn to stop. when the verse asked, wouldn't you love God to forgive you, he said yes, and went back to providing for Mistah.

original.note: Arabic, Qur'an 24:22: let them pardon, and let them overlook.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiveness is a feeling you wait for.
what it means: a withdrawn kindness, restored, because the verse asked: wouldn't you love to be forgiven?
what a scholar hears: Aisha's own account of the slander, the ifk, in Sahih al-Bukhari, with Qur'an 24:22 and Abu Bakr's yes.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4750 (the account of the ifk)
